prompt:

 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?

   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?

   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?

   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?

   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?

   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?

   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Boeing is a century-old incumbent in a mature duopoly, not a Rule Breaker leading an emerging industry. Its brand is famous but tarnished, its CEO is a hired turnaround manager, and the shares have fallen about 11% over the past year, so it shows few of Gardner's six traits.
summaries.buffett: Boeing has a duopoly position and a valuable services business, but Buffett's tests of consistent earnings, high returns on capital, low debt and honest, durable economics are not met: it lost money from 2019 to 2024, carries $45.9B of debt against $6.1B of equity, and trades at about 25 times book value with negative trailing free cash flow.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire the barriers to entry in large jets but, thinking backwards, see many ways to lose: safety failures, regulatory caps, fixed-price defense losses and a stretched balance sheet. The business is not simple to forecast, and paying for a turnaround that has yet to show sustained profits runs against his preference for great businesses at fair prices.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would classify Boeing as a turnaround: production is recovering (600 deliveries in 2025, 475 in the first nine months of 2026) and the story is simple, but earnings are still negative on a core basis, the share count has risen from 569M in 2020 to 791M, and its P/E cannot be compared with growth.
summaries.fisher: Boeing scores on Fisher's points for long-term sales potential ($715B backlog), R&D depth and a strong sales position with airlines, but recent R&D has produced late programs (777X, 737-7/10), profit margins are thin, labor relations have been poor and management candour was questioned after the 737 MAX crisis.
summaries.graham: Boeing fails most of Graham's defensive-investor criteria: it has not been profitable in each of the last ten years, suspended its dividend in 2020, EPS is far below its level of ten years ago, and its P/E times P/B is far above 22.5. Only its large size passes.
summaries.thiel: Boeing does not fit Zero to One: it is an incumbent in a two-player market with incremental rather than ten-times-better technology. Its durability comes from a duopoly that shelters it, but it has not found a unique new opportunity and its founder-era culture of breakthrough engineering has faded.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable compounders with rising free cash flow at reasonable prices; Boeing's trailing free cash flow is negative, margins are thin and it trades on hopes of a 2027-2028 recovery. The improving production ramp is a possible catalyst, but the setup is a turnaround bet rather than a high-quality compounder.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller focuses on what will look better in 18-24 months; Boeing's rising production rates, 777X entry and free cash flow guidance of $1-3B for 2026 could fit that, but earnings are not accelerating clearly, estimates have been cut (Morgan Stanley lowered its target in October 2026) and the shares lag the market.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith seeks high returns on capital, high gross margins and cash conversion with little debt; Boeing's 4.8% gross margin, negative ROIC, heavy debt and history of quality failures make it a poor fit for 'buy good companies'.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Boeing ranks poorly: its trailing operating profit (about $4.6B including a $9.6B one-off gain) is small against an enterprise value of about $176B, and its return on capital is negative excluding the gain.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool needs a great business, talented and honest managers and reinvestment at high returns; Boeing has a strong market position and a capable new CEO, but its returns on capital are negative and it cannot yet reinvest at high rates, so it does not fit.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai likes temporary, fixable problems with low downside; Boeing's troubles may be fixable and the duopoly limits the risk of extinction, but heavy debt, negative free cash flow and a price that already assumes recovery leave little 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much'.
summaries.wood: Boeing is not a disruptive-innovation platform in ARK's sense; its products are mature airframes, though autonomous aircraft (MQ-25, MQ-28) and space are adjacent to ARK themes. Its costs are not falling rapidly with volume, so it fits poorly.
summaries.ackman: Ackman seeks simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with dominant positions and high barriers to entry; Boeing has the barriers and dominance, but its predictability and free cash flow are currently weak, making it more of a turnaround idea than a core holding.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep favoured scale-economies-shared businesses that pass savings to customers; Boeing does not, as its scale advantages have been absorbed by production problems and its 10-20 year position is not clearly stronger than today given Airbus's lead.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge new markets created by technology shifts; Boeing serves a very large but old market, and it lacks the young, fast-growing opportunity Sequoia sought, so it fits poorly.
summaries.nash: Boeing fails most of Tom Nash's screens: more debt than cash, operating margin under 20%, negative trailing free cash flow, a weak balance sheet (liabilities 26 times equity) and a recent earnings miss. It scores about 60 of 130 on his 13 categories, and his DCF gives no support for today's price.

momentum.evidence: The shares closed at $190.21 on October 16, 2026, down about 11% over 52 weeks and near the low end of the $176.77-$254.35 range, lagging the market.

g4.evidence: CEO Kelly Ortberg is a respected aerospace engineer and former Rockwell Collins CEO, and institutions own about 73% of the shares, but there is no famous star investor or activist backing the stock.

g6.evidence: Some commentators call Boeing expensive (forward P/E above 200 on depressed earnings), but most analysts rate it a Buy with an average target of about $267.

simple.evidence: Building and selling airplanes is easy to grasp, but program accounting, fixed-price defense contracts and production-rate risk make results hard for a generalist to forecast.

b2.evidence: Boeing lost money every year from 2019 to 2024 and its 2025 profit of $2.2B relied on a $9.6B gain from selling Digital Aviation Solutions.

integrity.evidence: New management under Ortberg has been more candid about problems, but Boeing paid $200M to settle SEC charges in 2022 for misleading investors about the 737 MAX and entered a 2021 deferred prosecution agreement over a MAX fraud charge.

b6.evidence: Under Ortberg Boeing has shrunk to its core, selling Digital Aviation Solutions (Jeppesen) and buying back its main supplier Spirit AeroSystems in December 2025 to control quality rather than to build an empire.

roic.evidence: Return on invested capital is negative excluding one-off gains, and its reported return on equity is distorted by equity of only $6.1B against $45.9B of debt at June 30, 2026.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow was -$1.9B in 2025 and -$0.8B in the first half of 2026, and trailing twelve-month free cash flow through June 2026 was about -$0.2B.

b10.evidence: Boeing's diluted share count rose from 569.0M in 2020 to 790.6M in Q2 2026 while it lost money for years, and the share price is below its level of five years ago.

safety.evidence: With negative trailing free cash flow, a price-to-book ratio of about 25 and an enterprise value of about $176B, the price assumes a strong recovery rather than offering a margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: The shares trade at more than 200 times 2026 expected earnings and on negative free cash flow, so the price depends on 2027-2028 recovery targets being met.

mu5.evidence: The duopoly and US government support make outright failure unlikely, but safety lapses, FAA production limits, defense program losses and $45.9B of debt are several real ways to destroy value.

reinvest.evidence: Boeing is investing (a $1B expansion in North Charleston, new 737 lines in Everett) into a $715B backlog, but historical returns on these investments have been poor.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear turnaround: deliveries rose from 348 in 2024 to 600 in 2025, with 737 production moving to 47 a month and 787 to 10 a month.

ly3.evidence: Core earnings per share are still negative (consensus 2026 core EPS about -$1.10), so the P/E cannot be at or below a growth rate.

runway.evidence: A backlog of $715B at June 30, 2026 (over 6,700 airplanes) and analyst revenue forecasts rising from $89.5B in 2025 to about $124B in 2028 give years of growth.

ly7.evidence: Director Bradley Tilden bought 1,370 shares in May 2026, but insider buying is small and the share count has grown sharply since 2020 rather than shrinking.

ly8.evidence: Boeing is one of the most widely followed and covered stocks on Wall Street.

fi2.evidence: Boeing is developing the 777X, 737-7/10, F-47 fighter and MQ-25, but it has not committed to a clean-sheet replacement for the 737.

fi3.evidence: R&D of $3.6B in 2025 won the F-47 contract and keeps the 787 competitive, but the 777X and Starliner programs are years late and over budget.

fi4.evidence: Boeing took 1,167 gross airplane orders in 2025, more than Airbus's 1,000, showing strong sales relationships with airlines and lessors.

longterm.evidence: Ortberg has prioritised safety, quality and stable production over near-term deliveries, but Boeing's earlier history put buybacks and cost cuts ahead of engineering.

gr1.evidence: Boeing had $89.5B of revenue in 2025 and a market value of about $150B.

ni10.evidence: Boeing reported net losses every year from 2019 through 2024.

gr4.evidence: Boeing suspended its dividend in 2020 and pays none today.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS was $2.48 in 2025, far below the $17.85 Boeing earned in 2018 and its levels of a decade ago.

gr6.evidence: Average earnings over recent years are negative, so the price is not within 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 70 times a price-to-book ratio of about 25 is far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Boeing's jets compete closely with Airbus's on efficiency; neither has technology ten times better than the other.

timing.evidence: Strong air-travel demand, aircraft shortages and rising defense budgets favour Boeing now, but its own production and certification timing has repeatedly slipped.

th3.evidence: Boeing is a long-established player in a large global market rather than a company expanding from a niche.

team.evidence: Ortberg is a credible industry veteran, but the broader management team is still rebuilding after years of quality failures.

th5.evidence: Boeing has decades-long direct relationships with every major airline, lessor and the US Department of Defense.

durable.evidence: The cost and decade-long certification needed to build large jets mean Boeing's duopoly position with Airbus is very likely to hold in 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Boeing's opportunities in airplanes and defense are well known to everyone in the industry.

trend.evidence: Boeing benefits from long-term growth in air travel and rising defense spending, but not from a platform shift such as AI or cloud computing.

dr1.evidence: Losses are narrowing (core EPS -$0.76 in Q2 2026 vs -$1.24 a year earlier), but Q2 missed the -$0.28 consensus and firms such as Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs cut their targets in October 2026.

dr2.evidence: Higher 737 and 787 rates, 777X entry in 2027 and free cash flow expected to turn positive could make Boeing look better in 18-24 months, but much of this is in consensus forecasts.

dr4.evidence: Strong airline demand and defense budgets help, but high interest rates raise the cost of its $45.9B of debt and of customer financing.

dr6.evidence: Catalysts include Q3 2026 results on October 27, 737-7/10 certification, 777X certification and further production-rate increases.

dr7.evidence: Repeated delays, a weak balance sheet and execution risk make Boeing hard to justify as a large, concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin (revenue less cost of products and services) was only 4.8% in 2025.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing free cash flow is negative, and even the 2026 target of $1-3B would be a yield of only about 1-2% on a market value of about $150B.

gb2.evidence: Trailing operating profit of about $4.6B (including a $9.6B one-off gain) is under 3% of an enterprise value of about $176B.

pa2.evidence: Boeing's problems (quality lapses, FAA caps, strikes, supplier issues) look fixable, and production has recovered to 600 deliveries in 2025.

pa4.evidence: The duopoly and national-security importance limit the risk of collapse, but high debt and dilution from past equity raises could still cause permanent loss for shareholders.

wo1.evidence: Boeing is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing, though it works on autonomous aircraft.

wo2.evidence: Aircraft production costs are not falling quickly; Boeing has absorbed abnormal production costs and supplier inflation.

wo3.evidence: Its business rests on aerospace engineering rather than several converging innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Analysts expect revenue to grow about 11% a year to roughly $124B by 2028, not a many-times-larger market.

ac3.evidence: Boeing is exposed to airline cycles, interest rates, aluminium and titanium costs, tariffs and US defense budgets.

ns1.evidence: Boeing does not pass scale savings to customers in a way that strengthens its position; it has been losing share to Airbus.

ns4.evidence: If the turnaround succeeds Boeing could be stronger than today, but Airbus's lead in narrowbodies and COMAC's rise make that unclear.

va2.evidence: Boeing's planes and defense systems solve large, essential problems: moving people and cargo across the world and national security.

tn1.evidence: Boeing sells into steady air-travel and defense demand, not a new secular trend such as AI or energy, and it is an old business.

tn2.evidence: The market sees Boeing as a recovering aircraft maker, which is what it is; there is no hidden transformation.

tn3.evidence: Boeing is a large US company, but it is closely tied to the airline industry, one of Nash's zones to avoid.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew in 2025 (+34.5%) and 2025 was profitable only thanks to a $9.6B gain, while debt of $45.9B exceeds cash of $20.0B, so it passes at most two weakly.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was negative in several recent quarters (-$1.45B in Q1 2026) and debt has exceeded cash in every quarter.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 34.5% in 2025 and 10.7% in the first half of 2026, and consensus expects about 9% for full-year 2026.

tn7.evidence: First-half 2026 revenue growth of 10.7% plus a free-cash-flow margin of about -1.8% is far below 40.

tn8.evidence: In the first half of 2026 revenue rose 10.7% while total operating costs rose about 10.0%, lifting operating earnings from $285M to $604M.

tn9.evidence: Debt ($45.9B) exceeds cash ($20.0B) and operating margin is under 5%, both instant kills.

tn10.evidence: Boeing remains under close FAA oversight of 737 production and has faced a DOJ 737 MAX fraud case dating from a 2021 deferred prosecution agreement.

tn11.evidence: Boeing provides commercial jets, military aircraft and services that help airlines and governments move people and cargo and defend their countries, and charges per aircraft plus parts and service contracts.

tn13.evidence: Total about 60: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 10, operating margin 0, short interest (1.9%) 10, institutional ownership (73%) 10, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 0, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 0, secular trend 5, culture and mission 0, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue fell in 2024, operating margin was negative in 2020-2024, free cash flow was negative in 2020, 2021, 2024 and 2025, and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is under 2x, assets excluding goodwill ($148.3B) are below total liabilities ($159.8B), and liabilities are about 26 times equity, although the current ratio is 1.14.

tn18.evidence: Ortberg has run Boeing only since August 2024, is not a founder, and has no record of large open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: Boeing missed the Q2 2026 consensus, reporting a core loss of $0.76 a share against an expected $0.28.

tn21.evidence: There is no clown CEO or auditor change, but past misleading MAX disclosures (a $200M SEC settlement in 2022) and repeated program charges are red flags.

tn22.evidence: Boeing has large revenue, but weak fundamentals and big equity raises since 2020 have diluted shareholders, though it is not a hype stock.

tn24.evidence: An enterprise value of about $176B against negative trailing free cash flow implies a recovery to well over $10B of annual free cash flow, far above what Boeing delivers today.

tn25.evidence: Boeing's 3-year average free-cash-flow margin (2023-2025) is about -6%, so Nash's DCF gives a negative value even before subtracting $25.9B of net debt.

tn26.evidence: With 2026 core EPS expected to be negative, the forward P/E is not meaningful (above 200) and the PEG is far above 1 compared with peers such as Airbus and Lockheed Martin.
